title: Softening Language: Hedges & Downtoners
titleEs: Suavizar el mensaje: atenuadores y matizadores
summary: Give unwelcome news so that it is clear but not brutal: modal hedges (*may, might, could*), *seem / appear to*, *it looks as if*, downtoners (*slightly, a bit, somewhat*) and *not* + a positive word (*not ideal*). Hedge what is uncertain; keep the facts and the commitments firm.
canDo: Soften a negative fact with modals, *seem / appear to* and downtoners while keeping the fact itself clear.
Replace blunt words (*failed, bad, wrong*) with *not* + a positive word (*didn't go as well as we'd hoped, not ideal*).
Tell when hedging helps and when it becomes vague or evasive.
Hear and say the weak forms of *can, was* and *some*, and keep *can't* strong so that it is not mistaken for *can*.

focus.grammar: Hedging: may / might / could + bare infinitive · seem / appear + to-infinitive · it looks as if / it seems that + clause · downtoners (slightly, a bit, somewhat) · not + positive word (not ideal, not quite what we'd hoped) · I'm afraid + clause
focus.lexis: I'm afraid, not quite what we'd hoped, it looks as if, as far as we can tell, to be honest, not ideal, a bit of a, slightly, somewhat, fall short of, dress something up, a clearer picture
focus.afh: weak forms: can /kən/ vs strong can't /kænt/ · was /wəz/ (strong at the end: Yes, it was) · some /səm/ · a bit of a /ə ˈbɪt‿əv‿ə/ · slightly /ˈslaɪt.li/ without an extra vowel

warmup: Think of the last time someone gave you bad news: a doctor, a mechanic, a manager. Do you remember the exact words? Did they make the news easier to hear, or just harder to understand?

scenario.title: Search test: first results
scenario.context: The morning after the full-scale search test, Oliver sends the team a short summary. The decision on the search is due on Friday.
scenario.speaker: oliver
scenario.text: Hi all, here's a quick summary of yesterday's full-scale search test. {{I'm afraid}} the results {{weren't quite what we'd hoped}}. Under full load, searches took just over four seconds, twice our target, and the error rate was {{slightly}} higher than in the last run. {{It looks as if}} the indexing is the bottleneck, not the servers, but it {{might}} take a few days to confirm. {{To be honest}}, I don't think we can fix it properly before 20 June. That's {{not ideal}}, but it's better to know now. Full figures to follow this afternoon. Oliver
scenario.tts: Hi all, here's a quick summary [of](/əv/) yesterday's full-scale search test. I'm afraid the results weren't quite what we'd hoped. Under full load, searches took just over four seconds, twice our target, [and](/ənd/) the error rate [was](/wəz/) slightly higher than in the last run. It looks [as](/əz/) if the indexing is the bottleneck, not the servers, [but](/bət/) it might take a few days to confirm. To be honest, I don't think we [can](/kən/) fix it properly before the twentieth [of](/əv/) June. That's not ideal, [but](/bət/) it's better to know now. Full figures to follow this afternoon. Oliver

dialogue.title: Same facts, softer words
dialogue.context: Oliver has drafted a two-line message to Helen about the test. Ryan reads it before it goes out.

lines.speaker: ryan
lines.text: Oliver, your draft for Helen says: *The search failed the test. It won't be ready.* Is that the whole message?
lines.tts: Oliver, your draft [for](/fəɹ/) Helen says: The search failed the test. It won't be ready. Is that the whole message?

lines.speaker: oliver
lines.text: It's what happened. I'd rather not {{dress it up}}.

lines.speaker: ryan
lines.text: I'm not asking you to dress it up. But *failed* sounds {{a bit}} final, and we haven't decided anything yet.
lines.tts: I'm not asking you to dress it up. [But](/bət/) failed sounds a bit final, [and](/ənd/) we haven't decided anything yet.

lines.speaker: oliver
lines.text: Fair point. So what would you say? *The results {{weren't quite what we'd hoped}}?*
lines.tts: Fair point. So what [would](/wəd/) you say? The results weren't quite what we'd hoped?

lines.speaker: ryan
lines.text: Yes, and then the number: four seconds against a target of two. The number does the hard work; the softer words just set the tone.
lines.tts: Yes, [and](/ənd/) then the number: four seconds against a target [of](/əv/) two. The number does the hard work; the softer words just set the tone.

lines.speaker: oliver
lines.text: And *it won't be ready*? We can't promise that it will be.
lines.tts: [And](/ənd/) it won't be ready? We can't promise that it will be.

lines.speaker: ryan
lines.text: Then say it {{may not be}} ready for June 20, and say when we'll know. It {{seems to be}} the indexing, right?
lines.tts: Then say it may not be ready [for](/fəɹ/) June twentieth, [and](/ənd/) say when we'll know. It seems to be the indexing, right?

lines.speaker: oliver
lines.text: {{As far as we can tell}}. Okay: softer words, the same facts, and a date for the decision. I'll redo it.
lines.tts: [As](/əz/) far [as](/əz/) we [can](/kən/) tell. Okay: softer words, the same facts, [and](/ənd/) a date [for](/fə/) the decision. I'll redo it.

comprehension.q: Why does Ryan object to the word *failed*?
options: It sounds final, and nothing has been decided yet
It is grammatically wrong in this sentence
comprehension.explain: *Failed sounds a bit final, and we haven't decided anything yet.* The word claims more than the team knows.

comprehension.q: According to Ryan, what does "the hard work" in the message?
options: The number: four seconds against a target of two
comprehension.explain: *The number does the hard work; the softer words just set the tone.* Hedges never replace the facts.

comprehension.q: What will Oliver's new version contain?
options: Softer words, the same facts and a date for the decision
Fewer facts and a friendlier tone
A promise that the search will be ready
comprehension.explain: *Softer words, the same facts, and a date for the decision.*

chunks.def: a softened way to say that something was disappointing

chunks.def: it seems, judging by what we can see

chunks.def: to give the impression of being or doing something; appear is more formal

organizer.title: What did Oliver change?
organizer.prompt: Name the technique in each softened version: modal, downtoner, not + positive or introductory hedge.
rows: It didn't go as well as we'd hoped.

rows.hint: modal / downtoner / not + positive / introductory hedge
modal / downtoner / not + positive / introductory hedge

rows: It looks as if the indexing is the cause.

rows.hint: modal / downtoner / not + positive / introductory hedge

rows: The error rate was slightly higher.

rows.hint: modal / downtoner / not + positive / introductory hedge

organizer.explain: Four ways to soften: a modal lowers certainty (*may not*), an introductory hedge marks a conclusion (*it looks as if*), a downtoner makes a negative smaller (*slightly*), and *not* + a positive word replaces a harsh one (*didn't go as well as we'd hoped*).

questions.q: Compare the first draft and the message Oliver sent. Which facts are the same in both? What exactly has changed: the information, or how certain and how direct it sounds?
questions.model: The facts are the same: the test went badly (four seconds, twice the target), the cause is probably the indexing, and the search may miss 20 June. What changed is certainty and directness. *Won't* (certain) became *may not* (possible), because the decision has not been taken yet; *failed* became *didn't go as well as we'd hoped*, which sounds less final; and *it looks as if* presents the cause as a conclusion from evidence, not as a proven fact. Hedging adjusts certainty to what you really know. It does not remove facts.
criteria: You said the facts (the number, the probable cause, the risk to the date) did not change.
You said what changed is certainty (*won't* → *may not*) and directness (*failed* → *didn't go as well as we'd hoped*).
You linked the hedges to what is really known: the decision is not taken and the cause is not confirmed.

questions.q: Look at these softeners: *may not be*, *it looks as if the indexing is…*, *seems to slow down*, *slightly higher*, *didn't go as well as we'd hoped*. Write the pattern of each one: what comes after it (a bare verb, a full clause, a *to*-infinitive, an adjective)?
questions.model: *May / might / could* + bare infinitive: *may not be ready*. *It looks as if* + a full clause with its own subject and verb: *the indexing is the cause* (*it seems that* works the same way). *Seem / appear* + *to*-infinitive, with the real subject first: *the search seems to slow down*. A downtoner goes before an adjective or a comparative: *slightly higher*, *a bit slow*, *somewhat disappointing*. *Not* + a positive word replaces a negative one: *didn't go as well as we'd hoped* instead of *went badly*, *not ideal* instead of *bad*.
criteria: You gave modal + bare infinitive and *it looks as if* + full clause.
You gave *seem / appear* + *to*-infinitive with the real subject first.
You placed downtoners before an adjective or comparative and described *not* + a positive word.

questions.q: Ryan says the number does the hard work and the softer words only set the tone. The message ends with a firm *We'll know by Friday*. Why is that last sentence not hedged? What would happen to Helen's trust if every sentence were softened?
questions.model: Hedges belong where there is real uncertainty (the cause, the date); facts and commitments stay firm. *We'll know by Friday* is a promise the team can keep, so softening it (*we might possibly know at some point*) would sound evasive. Helen needs a message she can act on: the number shows how big the problem is, the hedges show honest uncertainty, and the firm date tells her when the decision will come. If every sentence is softened, she cannot tell what is known from what is a guess, and she starts to trust the message less, not more.
criteria: You said hedges go where there is real uncertainty, while facts and commitments stay firm.
You said *We'll know by Friday* is a commitment the team can keep, so it should not be hedged.
You said over-hedging sounds evasive and hides what is certain.

points: Hedging lowers the certainty of a statement to match what you really know: *won't* → *may not*, *is* → *seems to be*, *the cause is* → *it looks as if the cause is*.
Downtoners make a negative smaller (*slightly / a bit / somewhat higher*); *not* + a positive word replaces a harsh negative (*not ideal*, *didn't go as well as we'd hoped*).
Introductory phrases prepare the listener: *I'm afraid…*, *To be honest…*, *As far as we can tell…*.
Hedge the uncertainty, not the facts or the commitments: numbers and promises (*We'll know by Friday*) stay firm.
formulas: may / might / could (+ not) + bare infinitive
it looks as if / it seems that + clause · subject + seems / appears + to + verb
slightly / a bit / somewhat + adjective or comparative · not + positive word
rule.note: Spanish softens too (*parece que*, *un poco*, *me temo que*), so the instinct is right. The trap is the grammar: *parece que la búsqueda es lenta* becomes *the search seems to be slow* or *it seems that the search is slow*, never *the search seems that is slow*.

phonetics.intro: Las palabras funcionales (*can, was, some, of, a*) casi nunca llevan su vocal plena dentro de la frase: se reducen a schwa /ə/, la vocal neutra y relajada. Al dar malas noticias esto importa por partida doble: si dices *can* con vocal plena, el oyente puede entender *can't*; y si no reconoces la forma débil, te pierdes el matiz. Regla general: débil dentro de la frase; fuerte al final, en respuestas cortas o cuando se enfatiza.

items.meaning: be able to; be possible (here in its weak, unstressed form)

alerts.text: *Can* sin acento se reduce a /kən/: «kən», casi «kn». Si dices «KAN» con a plena, un nativo puede entender *can't*.
*Can't* lleva siempre vocal plena y acento: US /kænt/ «KANT», UK /kɑːnt/ «KAANT». La t final apenas se oye, así que la pista es la vocal: débil = sí se puede; plena = no se puede.
Al final o en respuestas cortas, *can* es fuerte: *Yes, we can* /kæn/. La reducción solo ocurre delante del verbo.

example.speaker: priya
example.text: We can't confirm the cause yet, but we can run the test again on Thursday.
example.tts: We can't confirm the cause yet, [but](/bət/) we [can](/kən/) run the test again on Thursday.

items.meaning: past of *be*, unstressed inside the sentence

variants.label: Weak was: /wəz/
variants.speaker: coach
variants.text: It was slower than we'd hoped.

alerts.text: Dentro de la frase, *was* es /wəz/: «uəz», con schwa. No «uos» con o plena.
Al final o en respuestas cortas es fuerte: *Yes, it was* /wʌz/ (US) · /wɒz/ (UK). Escucha las dos variantes.
La s final es sonora, /z/: «uəz», con zumbido. Igual en *is* y *as*.

example.speaker: oliver
example.text: The error rate was slightly higher than in the last run.
example.tts: The error rate [was](/wəz/) slightly higher than in the last run.

items.meaning: an amount or a number that is not stated

alerts.text: Delante de un sustantivo, *some* es /səm/: «səm», con vocal neutra y breve. No «SAM».
Es fuerte, /sʌm/, cuando significa «algunos, no todos» o va solo: *some of the pages*, *I'll take some*.
*Delays*: acento en LAY y s final sonora /z/: «di-LEIS», con zumbido.

example.speaker: alex
example.text: There may be some delays to the search, so let's plan for both dates.
example.tts: There may be [some](/səm/) [delays](/dɪlˈAz/) to the search, so let's plan [for](/fəɹ/) both dates.

items.meaning: a softened way to name a problem

alerts.text: Cuatro palabras en un solo bloque: «a-BI-ra-va», sin cortes. Solo *bit* lleva acento.
En EE. UU., la t de *bit* entre vocales suena como la r simple española: «BI-ra». En Reino Unido, t suave: «BI-ta».
*Of* es /əv/ y los dos *a* son /ə/. *Bit* lleva /ɪ/ breve: no «biit», que sería *beat*.

example.speaker: leo
example.text: It's a bit of a problem, but it's not the end of the world.
example.tts: It's a bit [of](/əv/) a problem, [but](/bət/) it's not the end [of](/əv/) the world.

items.meaning: a little; to a small degree

alerts.text: Empieza con /sl/: «SLAIT-li», sin e de apoyo. Nada de «es-LAIT-li».
La *gh* no suena: *slight* = «slait», igual que *light*, *right* o *might*.
/aɪ/ es el diptongo «ai» de *aire*. La t final de *slight* se corta antes de la l, pero no desaparece del todo.

structures.title: Modal hedges
structures.formula: may / might / could (+ not) + bare infinitive
structures.usage: A possibility, not a certainty: use it when the decision or the cause is still open.

examples.speaker: coach
examples.text: The search {{may not be}} ready for June 20.
examples.tts: The search may not be ready [for](/fəɹ/) June twentieth.

examples.speaker: alex
examples.text: The fix {{might take}} a few more days.

structures.title: Seem, appear, it looks as if
structures.formula: subject + seems / appears + to + verb · it looks as if / it seems that + clause
structures.usage: A conclusion drawn from what you can see, with room to be wrong. *Appear* is more formal than *seem*.

examples.speaker: priya
examples.text: The search {{seems to slow down}} under load.

examples.speaker: emma
examples.text: The indexing {{appears to be}} the main cause.

structures.title: Downtoners and not + positive
structures.formula: slightly / a bit / somewhat + adjective · not + positive word
structures.usage: Make a negative smaller without changing the fact. Do not use a downtoner to shrink a big number: *twice the target* is not *slightly* slower.

examples.speaker: oliver
examples.text: The error rate was {{slightly}} higher than in the last run.
examples.tts: The error rate [was](/wəz/) slightly higher than in the last run.

examples.speaker: ryan
examples.text: That's {{not ideal}}, but it's better to know now.
examples.tts: That's not ideal, [but](/bət/) it's better to know now.

l1.title: Seems that after a subject
l1.text: Spanish *la búsqueda parece que es lenta* has no word-for-word copy in English. Use the subject + *seems to*, or *it seems that* + a full clause.
l1.wrong: The search seems that is slow.
l1.right: The search seems to be slow. / It seems that the search is slow.

l1.title: Sincerely for «sinceramente»
l1.text: *Sincerely* closes a formal letter (*Yours sincerely*). To introduce an honest opinion, use *to be honest*, *honestly* or *frankly*.
l1.wrong: Sincerely, the results were not good.
l1.right: To be honest, the results weren't good.

l1.title: Maybe inside the verb
l1.text: *Maybe* is an adverb that starts the sentence. Inside the verb phrase, use the modal *may* or *might*.
l1.wrong: The search maybe will not be ready.
l1.right: The search may not be ready. / Maybe the search won't be ready.

l1.title: I think + negative
l1.text: English usually puts the negative on *think*, not on the second verb. It sounds softer and more natural.
l1.wrong: I think we can't fix it in time.
l1.right: I don't think we can fix it in time.

l1.title: Stacking softeners
l1.text: One or two hedges soften; four make the message vague. Choose the one that matches your real doubt.
l1.wrong: Maybe the results were possibly a little bit not so good.
l1.right: The results weren't quite what we'd hoped.

task.title: Bad feedback to a supplier, softened but clear
task.scenario: You work with Alex on the help-center project. Tom's agency has delivered the new article templates. In yesterday's review, about a third of the articles displayed badly on phones, mostly the long ones with tables. Next Friday's launch may have to move. Write a message to Tom: clear about the facts, soft in tone, firm about the next step.
task.brief: Give unwelcome feedback to a supplier with hedges and downtoners, without hiding the facts.
steps: Thank Tom and introduce the news with a softener.
Give the fact with a number.
Say what it may mean for the launch date.
Close with a firm request and a date.
keywords: as far as we can tell

chunks.label: not + positive
chunks.re: \bnot quite\b|\bweren't quite\b|\bas well as (we|i) ('d|had)\b|\bnot ideal\b|\bless than ideal\b

chunks.label: hedged cause
chunks.re: \b(looks|seems) as if\b|\bseems? to\b|\bappears? to\b|\bas far as (we|i) can tell\b|\bit seems that\b

extra.title: Extra: one formal sentence for the project sponsor
extra.brief: Summarise the problem in one formal sentence: an impersonal subject (*Initial testing suggests that…*), the fact with a number, and a modal for the consequence.

parts.speaker: alex
parts.text: Hi Tom, thanks for sending the new templates. {{I'm afraid}} the results of yesterday's review {{weren't quite what we'd hoped}}: {{about a third}} of the articles display badly on phones, mostly the long ones with tables. {{It looks as if}} the tables are wider than the screen, but we can't be sure yet. If that's the cause, the launch {{may need to}} move by a week. {{Could you}} take a look and send us a fix {{by Wednesday}}? I'll confirm the launch date on Thursday. Thanks, Alex
parts.label: Message to a supplier (neutral, written)
notes: *Thanks for sending…* and *I'm afraid…*: thanks first, then the softener prepares Tom for the news.
*Weren't quite what we'd hoped*: *not* + a positive idea instead of *bad* or *failed*.
*About a third of the articles*: the fact stays exact. The number carries the message, not the adjectives.
*It looks as if… but we can't be sure yet* and *may need to move*: hedges only where the team is genuinely unsure (the cause and the date).
*Could you… by Wednesday? I'll confirm… on Thursday*: the request and the commitment are firm, with dates.
parts.tts: Hi Tom, thanks [for](/fəɹ/) sending the new templates. I'm afraid the results [of](/əv/) yesterday's review weren't quite what we'd hoped: about a third [of](/əv/) the articles display badly on phones, mostly the long ones with tables. It looks [as](/əz/) if the tables are wider than the screen, [but](/bət/) we can't be sure yet. If that's the cause, the launch may need to move by a week. [Could](/kəd/) you take a look [and](/ənd/) send us a fix by Wednesday? I'll confirm the launch date on Thursday. Thanks, Alex

parts.speaker: emma
parts.text: {{Initial testing suggests that}} approximately one third of the articles {{do not display correctly}} on mobile devices; {{consequently}}, the launch date {{may need to be revised}}.
parts.label: One sentence for the sponsor (formal)
notes: *Initial testing suggests that*: the evidence is the subject, so nobody is blamed.
*Approximately one third*: the same fact in formal wording.
*Consequently* and *may need to be revised*: a formal linker and a modal passive for the consequence.
parts.tts: Initial testing suggests that approximately one third [of](/əv/) the articles do not display correctly on mobile devices; consequently, the launch date may need to be revised.

selfCheck.text: Si Tom lee tu mensaje, ¿sabe exactamente qué falló, cuánto y qué tiene que hacer y para cuándo? ¿O solo nota que estás preocupado? Copia la frase que lleva el dato principal.
¿Suavizaste el tono (*I'm afraid*, *weren't quite what we'd hoped*) sin pasar al registro de chat (*kind of*, *a bummer*) ni al de comité (*Initial testing suggests*)?
¿*Seem / appear* van con *to* + verbo, *it looks as if* con una oración completa, y los modales con el infinitivo sin *to* (*may need to move*, no *may needs*)?
¿Escribiste *seems that is*, *sincerely* por «sinceramente», *maybe will* o *I think we can't*? Debe ser *seems to be*, *to be honest*, *may / might* y *I don't think we can*.
¿Atenuaste solo lo que de verdad es incierto (la causa, la fecha) y mantuviste firmes el dato y la petición? Si hay más de dos atenuadores en una frase, ¿cuál sobra?
